contribution: Sound is described as a wave with a speed, a pitch and a timbre: the harmonic series is seen as an FFT spectrum, beats are calculated from the frequency difference, and the Doppler effect is derived from the geometry of the wavefronts separately for a moving source and a moving listener.
learn: describe pitch and timbre using frequency and the harmonic series, and classify infrasound and ultrasound.
make an FFT graph of a sound and read the fundamental frequency and the overtones from it.
explain beats and the Doppler effect and calculate the frequency heard.
prior: Sound is a longitudinal wave, and the speed of a wave is $v = f\lambda$ (chapter *How waves form and travel*)
When waves meet, their displacements add up (chapter *When waves combine: superposition and interference*)
The natural frequencies of a string and of a tube open at both ends are multiples of the fundamental frequency (chapter *Standing waves: nodes, antinodes and natural frequencies*)

activities.text: You are standing by the road when an ambulance drives past with its siren sounding. As the car approaches, the siren sounds bright and high. Just as the car passes you, the sound drops clearly lower and stays low as the car moves away. To the driver of the ambulance, the siren sounds the same all the time.
activities.question: How can the motion of the car change the pitch you hear, even though the siren itself does not change?

activities.title: Review: natural frequencies of a string
activities.prompt: The fundamental frequency of a guitar string is $110\,\text{Hz}$. At what other frequencies can a standing wave form on the string?

choices.text: $220\,\text{Hz}$, $330\,\text{Hz}$, $440\,\text{Hz}$ and so on.
choices.feedback: Correct. The natural frequencies of a string fixed at both ends are whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency, $f_n = n f_1$ (chapter *Standing waves: nodes, antinodes and natural frequencies*). Today we will see that the string sounds at all of these at the same time and that they decide the timbre of the sound.

choices.text: Only $330\,\text{Hz}$, $550\,\text{Hz}$, $770\,\text{Hz}$ and so on.
choices.feedback: Only the odd multiples belong to a tube closed at one end, which has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. Both ends of a string are nodes, so any whole number of half wavelengths fits on it and $f_n = n f_1$ with $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$

choices.text: $55\,\text{Hz}$, $27.5\,\text{Hz}$ and so on, because the wavelength can grow.
choices.feedback: The fundamental frequency is the *lowest* natural frequency of the string: the longest wave that fits on the string is $\lambda_1 = 2L$. The other natural frequencies are higher than it, whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency.

choices.text: At any frequency, as long as the string is plucked hard enough.
choices.feedback: Plucking harder changes the amplitude, not which standing waves fit on the string. The fixed ends are nodes, so a standing wave forms only at the natural frequencies $f_n = n f_1$.

activities.title: Prediction 1: an approaching siren
activities.prompt: Now the situation is different from the roadside at the start: you stand on the line of the road yourself, like listener A in the simulation, not at the side of the road. An ambulance drives at a steady speed straight towards you with its siren sounding. How does the frequency you hear change during the approach, before the car reaches you?

choices.text: The frequency stays the same throughout the approach and is higher than the siren's own frequency.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: when the source moves at $34\,\text{m/s}$, listener A hears $444\,\text{Hz}$ all the time, even though the source gets closer in the picture. The frequency depends on the speed of the source, not on the distance: in front of the source the wavefronts are steadily closer together ($\lambda_\text{A} = 0.765\,\text{m}$ instead of $0.85\,\text{m}$). A listener standing at the side of the road would hear the frequency slide downward already during the approach, because the speed of the car towards them decreases as the car passes.

choices.text: The frequency rises all the time as the car gets closer.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the reading $f_\text{A} = 444\,\text{Hz}$ stays the same all the way while the source moves at a steady $34\,\text{m/s}$. As the source approaches, the *loudness* grows, not the pitch. The frequency changes only when the speed changes: at $102\,\text{m/s}$ it is $571\,\text{Hz}$.

choices.text: The frequency is the same as the siren's own frequency; only the loudness grows.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: when the source moves at $34\,\text{m/s}$, listener A hears $444\,\text{Hz}$, not the frequency of the source, $400\,\text{Hz}$. In front of the source the wavefronts bunch together, because the source follows right behind the previous wavefront, so they reach the ear more often.

activities.title: Prediction 2: which one moves?
activities.prompt: A loudspeaker plays a sound with a frequency of $400\,\text{Hz}$. In situation 1 the loudspeaker moves at $102\,\text{m/s}$ towards a listener at rest. In situation 2 the loudspeaker is at rest and the listener moves towards it at the same speed. Which listener hears the higher frequency?

choices.text: Both hear an equally high frequency, because only the relative speed of the source and the listener matters.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: in front of a moving source the listener hears $571\,\text{Hz}$, but a moving listener hears only $520\,\text{Hz}$. Sound travels relative to the air, so it matters which one moves relative to the air. At low speeds the difference is small: at $34\,\text{m/s}$ the frequencies are $444\,\text{Hz}$ and $440\,\text{Hz}$.

choices.text: The listener towards whom the loudspeaker moves.
choices.feedback: The values of the model support this: $571\,\text{Hz}$ in front of the moving source and $520\,\text{Hz}$ for the moving listener. A moving source shortens the wavelength in front of it ($0.595\,\text{m}$). A moving listener does not change the wavelength ($0.85\,\text{m}$) but meets the wavefronts at the speed $v + v_\text{h}$.

choices.text: The listener who moves towards the loudspeaker.
choices.feedback: The values of the model refute this: the moving listener hears $520\,\text{Hz}$, but in front of the moving source the frequency is $571\,\text{Hz}$. The motion of the listener does not change the wavelength $0.85\,\text{m}$, but in front of a moving source the wavelength shortens to $0.595\,\text{m}$.

activities.text: A loudspeaker emits sound, and two listeners listen to it on different sides. Move the source or the listeners and follow the wavefronts and the frequencies heard.
activities.howto: Choose the *Situation*. When the *source moves*, the loudspeaker travels to the right towards listener A and away from listener B. When the *listeners move*, the loudspeaker is at rest and both listeners travel to the left: A towards the loudspeaker, B away from it. Adjust the frequency $f_0$ and the speed of the source. The grey circles are wavefronts, that is, compressions, and the orange ring at a listener's ear glows whenever a wavefront arrives. The readings show the frequency and the wavelength each listener hears in their direction, and the frequency bar below shows $f_\text{B}$, $f_0$ and $f_\text{A}$. The picture starts from the beginning, before the source and the listener meet. *Speed* changes only the pace of the animation.
activities.model: The speed of sound is $340\,\text{m/s}$ relative to still air, and there is no wind. The source and the listeners move along the same straight line at a steady speed that is less than the speed of sound. The picture is slowed down by a factor of about $400$, and in it one metre is $100$ pixels. Sound does not weaken on the way, and the model has no reflections. The frequencies are values calculated by the model, not measurements.
activities.calc: Wavefront $k$ leaves at the time $t_k = \tfrac{k}{f_0}$ from the point where the source is at that moment and travels at speed $v$. For two successive wavefronts the simulation solves the moment when the wavefront reaches a moving or a stationary listener. The frequency heard is one divided by the difference of these arrival times. The Doppler formula is not used; the result comes from the geometry of the wavefronts. The wavelength is the distance of two successive wavefronts at the same moment in the direction of the listener.

activities.title: Experiment 1: the source moves
activities.intro: Test prediction 1. The frequency of the loudspeaker is $400\,\text{Hz}$, and the loudspeaker moves towards listener A and away from listener B. Change only the speed of the source and record the speeds $0\,\text{m/s}$, $34\,\text{m/s}$ and $102\,\text{m/s}$ (each is a required row, because the feedback of the predictions uses them). Also watch whether $f_\text{A}$ changes as the loudspeaker gets closer to listener A in the picture.

activities.title: Experiment 2: the listeners move
activities.intro: Test prediction 2. The loudspeaker is now at rest and again plays a sound of $400\,\text{Hz}$. Listener A moves towards the loudspeaker and listener B away from it. Change only the speed of the listeners and record the same speeds $0\,\text{m/s}$, $34\,\text{m/s}$ and $102\,\text{m/s}$ as in experiment 1 (each is a required row). Compare the table with the table of experiment 1: which changes the frequency more, the motion of the source or of the listener? Does the wavelength change?

activities.title: Conclusion: why does the frequency change?
activities.prompt: On the basis of your tables, write: how do approaching and moving away change the frequency heard? Does the frequency change when the source comes closer at a steady speed? Why do a moving source and a moving listener not give exactly the same frequency at the same speed? Use the words wavelength and wavefront.
activities.model: When the source and the listener approach each other, the frequency heard is higher than $400\,\text{Hz}$, and when they move apart, lower. At a steady speed the frequency stays the same all the way, even though the distance changes: at $34\,\text{m/s}$ listener A heard $444\,\text{Hz}$ all the time from the moving source. In front of a moving source the wavefronts are closer together, because the source follows right behind the previous wavefront: the wavelength shortened from $0.85\,\text{m}$ to $0.765\,\text{m}$. When the listener moves, the wavelength stays $0.85\,\text{m}$, but the listener meets the wavefronts more often, and heard $440\,\text{Hz}$. The difference grows with the speed: at $102\,\text{m/s}$ the frequencies were $571\,\text{Hz}$ and $520\,\text{Hz}$. The values are calculated by the model, and in the model the air is at rest.
criteria: I say that approaching raises and moving away lowers the frequency heard, and I justify it with numbers from the table.
I say that at a steady speed the frequency does not depend on the distance.
I explain the effect of a moving source with the wavelength: the wavefronts bunch together in front of the source.
I explain that a moving listener does not change the wavelength but meets the wavefronts more often, and I compare the numbers of the tables.

activities.title: Read an FFT spectrum
activities.text: A student sang one long vowel and made an FFT graph of the sound (made-up sample data). The graph has five narrow peaks.

question.prompt: What is the fundamental frequency of the note, that is, the frequency that the ear hears as the pitch?

choices.text: $200\,\text{Hz}$, because the peaks are at its multiples.
choices.feedback: Correct. The peaks are at the frequencies $200$, $400$, $600$, $800$ and $1000\,\text{Hz}$, that is, at the members of the harmonic series $f_n = n \cdot 200\,\text{Hz}$. The fundamental frequency is the spacing of the peaks and the frequency of the lowest peak, even though in this sound the second partial is the strongest.

choices.text: $400\,\text{Hz}$, because it is the highest peak of the spectrum.
choices.feedback: The highest peak tells which partial is the strongest, not the pitch. All the peaks are at multiples of $200\,\text{Hz}$, so the sound is a harmonic series with the fundamental frequency $200\,\text{Hz}$. A strong second partial affects the timbre.

choices.text: $1000\,\text{Hz}$, because it is the greatest frequency of the spectrum.
choices.feedback: The greatest frequency is the fifth partial, $5 \cdot 200\,\text{Hz}$. The pitch is decided by the lowest frequency of the harmonic series, the fundamental frequency, and the overtones change the timbre.

choices.text: $600\,\text{Hz}$, because it is the average of the frequencies of the peaks.
choices.feedback: The average of the frequencies has no meaning here: the ear hears the fundamental frequency of the harmonic series. The spacing of the peaks, $200\,\text{Hz}$, is the fundamental frequency.

activities.title: Make an FFT graph yourself
activities.prompt:
Make an FFT graph of a sound with the school's measuring program (for example Graphical Analysis) and a microphone or a sound sensor. The steps are the same whatever the program:

1. Connect the microphone and check that the program shows the pressure or the sound signal as a function of time.
2. Choose a high sampling rate, for example $20\,000$ samples per second, and a short measuring time, for example $0.1\,\text{s}$. The sampling rate must be at least twice the greatest frequency that you want to see.
3. Sound the note close to the microphone: strike a tuning fork, play a long note on an instrument or sing a vowel. Start the measurement when the sound is steady.
4. Check the time graph: it must show a periodic curve that is not clipped at the top or the bottom.
5. Choose FFT as the type of the graph. Read the frequencies of the peaks, for example with the examine tool.

If you do not have a microphone, use this made-up sample data: a $440\,\text{Hz}$ tuning fork, one peak at $440\,\text{Hz}$; the same note sung, peaks at $440$, $880$, $1320$ and $1760\,\text{Hz}$ with strengths in the ratio $1.0 : 0.6 : 0.4 : 0.2$. Otherwise measure at least two sounds, for example a tuning fork and your own voice on the same note. Record for each the fundamental frequency and the frequencies of the next three peaks. Are they multiples of the fundamental frequency? How do the spectra differ, and what does the difference tell about timbre?
activities.model: For example, the spectrum of a $440\,\text{Hz}$ tuning fork has one clear peak at about $440\,\text{Hz}$. When a singer sings the vowel a on the same note, the spectrum has peaks at about $440\,\text{Hz}$, $880\,\text{Hz}$, $1320\,\text{Hz}$ and $1760\,\text{Hz}$, that is, at whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency. The pitch is the same, because the fundamental frequency is the same. The timbre is different, because the singing has strong overtones and the tuning fork has almost none. The measured frequencies differ by a few hertz: with a measuring time of $0.1\,\text{s}$ the spectrum resolves frequencies only at intervals of about $\tfrac{1}{0.1\,\text{s}} = 10\,\text{Hz}$.
criteria: I recorded for both sounds the fundamental frequency and the frequencies of at least three other peaks.
I checked by calculation whether the peaks are multiples of the fundamental frequency.
I explained the difference of the spectra with timbre, that is, with the strengths of the overtones.
I assessed the accuracy of the measurement, for example the effect of the measuring time or the background noise.

activities.title: Read beats from a graph
activities.text: Two tuning forks sound at the same time, and a microphone records their combined sound for one second. The beat frequency is how many times per second the sound grows louder. The vibration is so dense that in the graph it appears as a filled area; the width of the area tells how strong the sound is at each moment.

question.prompt: How large is the beat frequency $f_\text{h}$? Read the time you need from the graph and give the answer in hertz.
hints: A loud moment is where the filled area is at its widest. At which moments are there such points?
The time between two successive loud moments is the period of the beats $T_\text{h}$, and $f_\text{h} = \tfrac{1}{T_\text{h}}$.

mistakes.feedback: You read the time as $0.50\,\text{s}$, but there are loud moments also at $0.25\,\text{s}$ and $0.75\,\text{s}$. The period of the beats is the time between two *successive* loud moments, $0.25\,\text{s}$.
$0.25\,\text{s}$ is the period of the beats $T_\text{h}$. The beat frequency is its reciprocal, $f_\text{h} = \tfrac{1}{T_\text{h}}$.

question.solution:
**Given:** from the graph, the loud moments (filled area at its widest) are $t = 0$, $0.25$, $0.50$, $0.75$ and $1.00\,\text{s}$

**Find:** the beat frequency $f_\text{h}$ in hertz

**Principle:** Two sounds of almost the same frequency reinforce each other when they are in phase and weaken each other when they are in opposite phase. The time between the loud moments is the period of the beats $T_\text{h}$, and the number of loud moments per second is $f_\text{h}$.

**Reading the graph:** The filled area is at its widest at the moments $0\,\text{s}$, $0.25\,\text{s}$, $0.50\,\text{s}$, $0.75\,\text{s}$ and $1.00\,\text{s}$. So there are four intervals in a second, and the time between two successive loud moments is $T_\text{h} = 0.25\,\text{s}$.

**Formula:** $f_\text{h} = \dfrac{1}{T_\text{h}}$

**Conversions:** The time is already in seconds, so the frequency comes out in hertz ($\tfrac{1}{\text{s}} = \text{Hz}$).

**Substitution:** $f_\text{h} = \dfrac{1}{0.25\,\text{s}} = 4.0\,\text{Hz}$

**Answer:** $4.0\,\text{Hz}$, two significant figures like the time $0.25\,\text{s}$ read from the graph.

**Reasonableness:** The graph has four narrowing points per second and four intervals between loud moments, which corresponds to four beats per second. If one of the tuning forks is $440\,\text{Hz}$, the other is, by $f_\text{h} = |f_1 - f_2|$, either $436\,\text{Hz}$ or $444\,\text{Hz}$; the difference is less than $10\,\text{Hz}$, so the beats are clearly audible.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the values of the model in the experiments and with the Doppler formulas. How does the situation of prediction 1 (you stand on the line of the car) differ from the roadside at the start, where the frequency slides? Then return to the question at the start: why does the siren sound as if it drops in pitch just at the moment of passing? Why does the siren sound the same to the driver all the time?

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt:
A moped approaches a listener at $20.0\,\text{m/s}$, and the frequency of its horn is $620\,\text{Hz}$. A student calculates the frequency heard like this:

$$\begin{aligned} f &= f_0 \cdot \frac{v}{v + v_\text{s}} \\ &= 620\,\text{Hz} \cdot \frac{340\,\text{m/s}}{360\,\text{m/s}} \\ &\approx 586\,\text{Hz} \end{aligned}$$

Where is the error?

choices.text: The sign is wrong: for an approaching source the denominator is $v - v_\text{s}$, and the correct result is about $659\,\text{Hz}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. Approaching raises the frequency heard, but the student's result $586\,\text{Hz}$ is lower than $620\,\text{Hz}$. When the source approaches, the wavefronts bunch together in front of it and the wavelength is $(v - v_\text{s}) T_0$, so $f = 620\,\text{Hz} \cdot \tfrac{340}{320} \approx 659\,\text{Hz}$.

choices.text: The formula is wrong: when the moped moves, the listener's formula must be used, because the listener is the one who measures.
choices.feedback: The choice of the formula depends on which one moves relative to the air. Here the source moves, so the moving-source formula is the right one. The error is in the sign: the result $586\,\text{Hz}$ is lower than $f_0$ even though the moped approaches.

choices.text: The speed of the moped must be added to the speed of sound, because the moped pushes the sound forward.
choices.feedback: Sound always travels relative to the air at $340\,\text{m/s}$, whether the source moves or not. The motion of the moped changes the wavelength in front of it, not the speed of sound. The error is in the sign of the denominator.

choices.text: There is no error in the calculation: the sound of an approaching source sounds lower, because the wavefronts stretch.
choices.feedback: The wavefronts stretch *behind* the source. In front of an approaching source they bunch together, the wavelength shortens and the frequency heard grows. The result $586\,\text{Hz} < 620\,\text{Hz}$ should have raised suspicion.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: A student whirls a buzzer tied to the end of a string in a horizontal circle of radius $1.00\,\text{m}$. One revolution takes $0.500\,\text{s}$, and the frequency of the buzzer is $2.00\,\text{kHz}$. A listener standing far away in the same plane hears the pitch vary. What is the greatest frequency the listener hears? The air is calm, and the speed of sound is $340\,\text{m/s}$. Answer in hertz.
hints: At which point of the circle does the buzzer move straight towards the listener? How large is its speed then?

In uniform circular motion the speed is $v_\text{s} = \tfrac{2\pi r}{T}$ (chapter *Moving in a circle: period and speed*). The greatest frequency is heard when the buzzer approaches the listener at this speed.

mistakes.feedback: This is the *lowest* frequency heard, which is heard when the buzzer moves away from the listener. For an approaching source the denominator is $v - v_\text{s}$.
You used $\tfrac{r}{T}$ as the speed. The length of one revolution is the circumference of the circle, $2\pi r$, so the speed is $v_\text{s} = \tfrac{2\pi r}{T} = 12.57\,\text{m/s}$.

$2000\,\text{Hz}$ is the buzzer's own frequency. The listener hears it only when the buzzer moves sideways relative to the direction of the listener. When the buzzer moves straight towards the listener, the frequency is higher.

activities.solution:
**Given:** radius of the circle $r = 1.00\,\text{m}$, period of revolution $T = 0.500\,\text{s}$, frequency of the buzzer $f_0 = 2.00\,\text{kHz}$, speed of sound $v = 340\,\text{m/s}$

**Find:** the greatest frequency heard $f$ in hertz

**Principle:** The buzzer moves in a circle at a steady speed, and the distant listener is in the plane of the circle. The frequency heard is affected only by the part of the velocity that points towards the listener or away from them. The greatest frequency is heard when the buzzer moves straight towards the listener with its whole speed. The listener is at rest, so we use the moving-source formula with the sign for approaching.

**Formula:** $v_\text{s} = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$ and $f = f_0 \cdot \dfrac{v}{v - v_\text{s}}$, so $f = f_0 \cdot \dfrac{v}{v - \tfrac{2\pi r}{T}}$

**Conversions:** $f_0 = 2.00\,\text{kHz} = 2000\,\text{Hz}$; the other quantities are in base units.

**Substitution:** $v_\text{s} = \dfrac{2\pi \cdot 1.00\,\text{m}}{0.500\,\text{s}} = 12.566\,\text{m/s}$ and $f = 2000\,\text{Hz} \cdot \dfrac{340\,\text{m/s}}{340\,\text{m/s} - 12.566\,\text{m/s}} = 2076.8\,\text{Hz}$

**Answer:** $2.08\,\text{kHz}$, that is, about $2080\,\text{Hz}$, three significant figures like the radius, the period and the frequency.

**Reasonableness:** The speed of the buzzer is about $\tfrac{12.6}{340} \approx 3.7\,\%$ of the speed of sound, so the frequency rises by about $3.7\,\%$, that is, about $75\,\text{Hz}$. When the buzzer moves away, the frequency is correspondingly about $1929\,\text{Hz}$, so the listener hears the sound waver between about $1930\,\text{Hz}$ and $2080\,\text{Hz}$ twice a second.

activities.text: Practise on three levels. Level 1 tasks use one formula, level 2 tasks need two steps or a unit conversion, and level 3 requires reasoning.

activities.title: 1. A moving listener
activities.prompt: A cyclist rides towards a church bell at rest that sounds at a steady frequency. The cyclist hears the sound of the bell higher than a person standing in the churchyard. Which explanation is correct?

choices.text: The cyclist meets the wavefronts more often, because the cyclist moves towards them, even though the wavelength does not change.
choices.feedback: Correct. When the source is at rest, the spacing of the wavefronts is the same everywhere, $\lambda = \tfrac{v}{f_0}$. Relative to the cyclist the wavefronts approach at the speed $v + v_\text{h}$, so they arrive more often: $f = f_0 \cdot \tfrac{v + v_\text{h}}{v}$.

choices.text: In front of the cyclist the wavelength is shorter, because their motion squeezes the wavefronts closer together.
choices.feedback: The wavefronts are created at the source, and the church bell is at rest, so the spacing of the wavefronts is the same everywhere. The cyclist does not change the wavelength; they only meet the wavefronts more often. The wavelength shortens only in front of a moving *source*.

choices.text: The speed of sound increases when the cyclist rides towards it, and faster sound sounds higher.
choices.feedback: Sound travels relative to the air at the speed $v$. *Relative to* the cyclist the wavefronts approach at the speed $v + v_\text{h}$, and that is why the cyclist meets them more often. Pitch depends on the frequency, that is, on how often the wavefronts reach the ear, not on the speed of sound as such.

choices.text: The bell vibrates faster, because the cyclist approaches it.
choices.feedback: The bell's own frequency $f_0$ does not depend on who is listening: a person standing in the churchyard hears the same frequency all the time. The change comes from the motion of the cyclist relative to the air.

activities.title: 2. Measuring the speed of sound
activities.prompt: Two microphones are placed $1.20\,\text{m}$ apart on the same straight line as a loudspeaker. The loudspeaker emits a short click, and from the signals recorded by the measuring program it is read that the click arrives at the farther microphone $3.50\,\text{ms}$ later than at the nearer one. What is the speed of sound according to the measurement? Answer in m/s.
hints: What distance does the sound travel in the time in which the click goes from the nearer microphone to the farther one?
Sound travels the distance $d$ between the microphones in the time $\Delta t$, so $v = \tfrac{d}{\Delta t}$.

mistakes.feedback: You forgot to convert milliseconds to seconds: $3.50\,\text{ms} = 0.00350\,\text{s}$. Your result is in m/ms.
You multiplied the distance by two as in the echo measurement. Here the sound does not return, but travels the distance between the microphones, $1.20\,\text{m}$, only once.

activities.solution:
**Given:** distance of the microphones $d = 1.20\,\text{m}$, difference in arrival times $\Delta t = 3.50\,\text{ms}$

**Find:** the speed of sound $v$ in m/s

**Principle:** The microphones are on the same straight line as the loudspeaker, so the sound travels to the farther microphone the same distance as to the nearer one and in addition the distance $d$ between the microphones. The time difference $\Delta t$ is therefore the time in which sound travels the distance $d$ at a steady speed.

**Formula:** $d = v \Delta t$, so $v = \dfrac{d}{\Delta t}$

**Conversions:** $3.50\,\text{ms} = 3.50 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\text{s}$

**Substitution:** $v = \dfrac{1.20\,\text{m}}{3.50 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\text{s}} = 342.86\,\text{m/s}$

**Answer:** $343\,\text{m/s}$, three significant figures like the distance and the time difference.

**Reasonableness:** The result matches the table value $343\,\text{m/s}$ for air at $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, that is, room temperature. If the time difference were misread by $0.05\,\text{ms}$, the result would change by about $5\,\text{m/s}$, so reading the time difference accurately decides the accuracy of the measurement.

activities.title: 3. Explain timbre
activities.prompt: A violin and a flute play the same note with the fundamental frequency $440\,\text{Hz}$, and yet they sound different. Explain what is the same and what is different in the sounds, and how the difference would show in their FFT graphs. Use the concepts fundamental frequency, overtone and harmonic series.
criteria: I say that the pitch is the same, because the fundamental frequency is the same.
I say that both sounds contain overtones whose frequencies form the harmonic series $f_n = n f_1$.
I explain that timbre depends on the strengths of the overtones, so the spectra of the instruments are different.
I describe the FFT graphs: the peaks are at the same frequencies but with different heights.
activities.model: Both sounds have the fundamental frequency $440\,\text{Hz}$, so the ear hears the same pitch. However, both instruments also vibrate at their overtones at the same time. These are the multiples of the fundamental frequency, $880\,\text{Hz}$, $1320\,\text{Hz}$ and so on, and they form the harmonic series $f_n = n f_1$. Timbre depends on how strong the overtones are compared with the fundamental frequency, and it is different for different instruments. In the FFT graphs both have peaks at the same frequencies, but the heights of the peaks are different: in the sound of the violin there are strong overtones far up the series, in the sound of the flute the fundamental frequency dominates and the overtones are weaker.

activities.text: Finally, two quick questions. Answer first yourself and open the answer only afterwards.
